nameStory: The 'great' in great coneflower refers to its impressive size - this towering member of the coneflower family can reach up to eight feet tall, making it a true giant among its black-eyed Susan cousins. The 'coneflower' part comes from the plant's distinctive raised center that forms a prominent cone shape, like a little brown hat sitting atop the flower.
description: Great coneflower is a dramatic, towering wildflower that can reach an impressive eight feet in height. It produces large daisy-like flowers with bright yellow petals surrounding a prominent dark brown cone-shaped center. This member of the sunflower family is primarily grown as an ornamental plant in New England gardens. Its seeds attract finches and other small songbirds who come to feast on the nutritious bounty.

idTips.description: Exceptionally tall plant reaching up to 8 feet - towers above most other wildflowers and garden perennials

idTips.label: Flowers

habitat: In New England, great coneflower is primarily found in cultivated gardens and ornamental plantings rather than wild habitats. It thrives in sunny locations with well-drained soil and is often planted in perennial borders, prairie-style gardens, and naturalized areas where its impressive height can be showcased.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with large leaves developing on sturdy stems that will eventually reach impressive heights.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with showy yellow flowers displaying their characteristic dark cone centers.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature in the cone centers, attracting finches and other seed-eating birds. Spent flower heads persist.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems and seed heads may remain standing, providing winter interest and continued food for birds.

funFact: Great coneflower is like a natural bird feeder - finches and other small birds will actually perch right on the sturdy cone centers to crack open and eat the seeds, sometimes creating quite a lively feeding party in late summer and fall!
confusionNotes: The massive 8-foot height immediately separates great coneflower from its shorter relatives like black-eyed Susan (2-3 feet) and orange coneflower (1-3 feet). Remember: if you have to crane your neck to see the flowers clearly, you're probably looking at a great coneflower!
contextualKnowledge: With only 5 recorded observations in New England, great coneflower is quite rare in the region and is primarily encountered in specialized gardens or cultivated settings rather than growing wild like many of its more common Rudbeckia relatives.
compareHints: Great coneflower's towering 8-foot height immediately distinguishes it from all other Rudbeckia species in New England - black-eyed Susan tops out around 3 feet, cutleaf coneflower reaches about 4-6 feet, and orange coneflower stays under 3 feet. While they all share the classic yellow petals and dark cone centers, great coneflower is literally head and shoulders above the rest.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Rudbeckia relatives, black-eyed Susan is distinguished by its rough, hairy texture and moderate size.

Among the Rudbeckia family, cutleaf coneflower is the giant with the fancy haircut - it's much taller than black-eyed Susan and has those distinctive deeply-divided leaves that no other coneflower possesses.
Among the Rudbeckia family, brown-eyed Susan stands out for its smaller flowers and brown (not black) centers.
Orange coneflower differs from black-eyed Susan by forming spreading colonies rather than individual clumps, and has slightly more orange-tinted petals.
Among its Rudbeckia relatives, sweet black-eyed Susan stands out for its impressive height and fragrant flowers.
Unlike its Rudbeckia cousins, clasping coneflower has small chaffy scales (like tiny bracts) beneath its ray petals that other black-eyed Susans lack.
